# The Cartographer's Compass

## Tromsø

The rain in Tromsø never really fell so much as it hung in the air, a fine mist that coated everything in a perpetual sheen. Bruno stood at the edge of the harbor, the quill in his pocket already beginning to feel heavy with promise. He had come here chasing a rumor—a rumor that the old cartographers' guild still kept records of routes that no modern map would ever chart.

The quill had been his grandmother's, a thing of black feather and silver ferrule, and she had told him before she died that it would lead him to the places where the world's edges were still being drawn. He'd laughed at the time. Now, standing in this gray Norwegian town, he wasn't so sure.

He found the guildhall on a narrow street that climbed too steeply for the cobblestones to have survived a century. Inside, an old woman with ink-stained fingers looked at the quill and wept.

"You carry her handiwork," she said. "And she carried ours. There is a map, Bruno. A map that was never finished. It begins here, in the place where the northern lights touch the sea, but it does not end here. It ends in two places that should not exist together." She pressed a folded sheet into his hands. "Follow the ink. It always knows where it is going."

Bruno unfolded the map. It was blank, save for a single dot of black ink in the upper left corner, pulsing faintly like a heartbeat. And when he looked up, the mist outside seemed to part, just slightly, as if the town itself were holding its breath.

## Cusco

The altitude hit him first—thin, fierce air that made his lungs burn and his thoughts sharpen. Cusco sat high in the Andes, a city built on the bones of an empire, its stone walls older than the memory of the people who now walked its streets.

Bruno followed the ink dot down and across an ocean, and it led him to a small shop in the old quarter, where a woman named Elif was sorting anchors into crates. Not ship's anchors—she made them, these, of a peculiar blue metal that never tarnished. She looked up as he entered, and without a word, she reached into a drawer and pulled out an anchor, small enough to fit in a palm, and held it out to him.

"You're looking for the map," she said. It wasn't a question. "My grandmother told me someone would come. She said to give you this." She turned the anchor over in her hands. "She said it would open the second door."

Bruno looked at the map. The ink dot had moved—it was no longer in the corner, but somewhere in the middle, and it had grown. He looked from the anchor to Elif's face.

"Why are you helping me?"

"Because my grandmother left me an anchor and a promise, just as yours left you a quill and one." She smiled, and it was a sad, knowing smile. "The map needs three things to be completed. A quill to write it, an anchor to hold it down, and an atlas to carry it. You have two. You need the third."

## Oaxaca

The desert heat of Oaxaca was a shock after the Andean chill. Bruno arrived by a route he no longer remembered planning, the map folded in his coat, the anchor in his pocket, the quill in his hand. The ink dot had grown into a small black sun by now, warm against his skin whenever he thought of it.

The atlas was kept in a library that smelled of dust and vanilla and old paper. Its keeper was a man named Farid, who had been waiting, it seemed, for far longer than Bruno had been traveling.

"You're late," Farid said, not unkindly, as Bruno entered. He set down the book he'd been reading—a book with blank pages, Bruno realized, waiting to be filled. "But you're here. That's what matters."

Bruno placed the quill and the anchor on the counter between them. Farid's eyes moved between the two objects, and then to the map.

"Two of three," he said. "The quill that writes. The anchor that holds. But the map has no place to go. It has no atlas." He opened the blank book, and inside, for the first time, words began to form—
